title: Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment
author: Nadia Sussman
content:
Earlier this year, we heard that reporter Jake Pearson planned to ask our
editors at ProPublica for more than $20,000 so he could spend the NBA playoffs
[betting like a problem
gambler](https://www.propublica.org/article/draftkings-sports-gambling-
problem-vip-fanduel).

We told him we wanted in on the action.

For 10 weeks, our documentary team at ProPublica filmed Jake as he dove ball-
cap-first into DraftKings and FanDuel, the country’s largest online
sportsbooks. Jake bet early, late and often, ramping up the amounts and
frequency of his wagers, chasing his losses with even bigger bets.  He wanted
to flagrantly wave the red flags of a gambler descending into addiction. Would
the apps serve up speed bumps as he careened into the red, or would they push
him to keep betting?

Since 2018, the year the Supreme Court opened the door for states to legalize
sports betting, the number of people staking money on games has exploded. It’s
now legal in 39 states and Washington, D.C. The apps don’t just offer straight
action on the outcome of a “Sunday Night Football” game — you can put money on
myriad sports events and outcomes, including who will score the next point in
a tense contest of Czech table tennis. Every month, millions do.

More than $600 billion has sloshed through the legal sportsbooks in wagers —
and brought billions in state tax revenue — in the last eight years. But
between the ever-present ads featuring celebrities from LeBron James and
Charles Barkley to Kevin Hart and Kendall Jenner, cracks in the system have
started to show.

About a quarter of active sportsbook account holders surveyed by the Siena
Research Institute this year said that they’d lost enough on a bet that they’d
have [trouble meeting their financial
obligations](https://sri.siena.edu/2026/04/13/more-than-a-quarter-of-
americans-27-have-an-active-online-sports-betting-account-a-third-have-opened-
an-account-at-least-once/). Other studies and public health experts warn of
rising cases of bankruptcy, addiction and self-harm.

![A man wearing a backward baseball cap sits in a dark bar, staring at his
phone.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Sportsbetting_Pearson_FilmStill_BettingBar_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg)ProPublica
reporter Jake Pearson at a Manhattan bar this spring, testing DraftKings’ and
FanDuel’s guardrails. More than a quarter of people in the U.S. say they have
an active account with an online sportsbook, according to a poll by the Siena
Research Institute. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica

DraftKings and FanDuel say that they don’t want to profit off bettors who
can’t control themselves, and they provide a range of what the industry calls
“responsible gaming” tools to help users stay in check.

Jake received pop-up notices, reminders and emails noting his time on the app
and nudging him to “take a beat” after a loss. He opted into some of the tools
DraftKings makes available. But he was struck by user design choices and
promotions that encouraged him to keep betting, some of which he was served
right after setting limits on his play.

In a statement, DraftKings told ProPublica that it trains its more than 5,000
employees on responsible gaming and has more than 50 full-time staff dedicated
to its “responsible engagement” program. A FanDuel spokesperson wrote that the
company’s program is “designed to identify potential risk early and empower
customers with real-time information about their play.”

Even so, regulators and lawmakers from Colorado to Massachusetts have begun to
question whether sportsbooks have sufficient protections in place. Those
concerns have risen with the popularization of prediction markets, which are
even less regulated than sports betting apps like DraftKings.

We were behind the camera back in April when Jake opened his DraftKings
account to place his first bet, a $100 Hail Mary wager for the New York Knicks
to win the chip. We had no idea what a ride it would be.  

**[Watch our new documentary](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l8IyGjdY1sg)
that follows Jake as he intentionally descends into problem gambling — and see
how the apps react. **

**Have you used apps like DraftKings or FanDuel to place sports bets?**
ProPublica is looking for at least 250 people who use these apps to [share
their data](https://projects.propublica.org/sports-betting-uploader/) with us.
Your transaction history will help us better understand how the apps respond
to user behavior. You can also reach Jake Pearson and the reporting team at
917-512-0276 or
[sportsbetting@propublica.org](mailto:sportsbetting@propublica.org).

The post [Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting
Experiment](https://www.propublica.org/article/sports-betting-problem-
gambling-draftkings-fanduel) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
